Definition: Whether individuals can view their data held in the ID database and see how it has been accessed
Comments: The Data Protection Act 2022 grants individuals the right of access to their personal data and the right to challenge its accuracy, as well as the right to correction or deletion. This provides a legal basis for individual data access. However, a practical self-service portal for ID data access does not appear to exist; the right is exercised through the ESCCOM/EDPA.
revision_notes: Fetched and read both cited sources plus the primary Gazette text of the Act. Confirmed: Data Protection Act, 2022 (Act No. 5 of 2022, in force 4 March 2022) ss.19-20 grant data subjects the right to access and challenge the accuracy of their personal data, with correction/deletion rights. No dedicated self-service ID data portal identified; the right is exercised via requests to data controllers or complaints to ESCCOM as Data Protection Authority. Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed.
revised_comments: Eswatini's Data Protection Act, 2022 (Act No. 5 of 2022), in force from 4 March 2022, grants individuals the right to access their personal data held by data controllers, to challenge its accuracy, and to request correction or deletion. There is no dedicated self-service ID data portal; individuals exercise these rights through requests to data controllers or complaints to the Eswatini Communications Commission acting as the Data Protection Authority.

Definition: Whether the system enables Know Your Customer (KYC) packet collection for service provision, particularly financial services
Comments: Commercial banks can access the civil registry for identity verification, enabling KYC processes using the national ID. The APC 2024 report notes 'recent developments allowing service providers like commercial banks to access the civil registry for identity verification.' Smile ID confirms the national ID card is the primary KYC document in Eswatini for financial services. The 2022 AML/KYC regulations under Section 19 of the Money Laundering Act require ID-based KYC. DPI Map records 'Enables KYC: NO' for fully digital KYC, but physical ID-based KYC is operational.
revision_notes: DPI Map (last updated Oct 2024) explicitly records 'Enables KYC packet collection: NO'. Independent news reporting corroborates this: as of September-October 2025 the Central Bank of Eswatini was only beginning to develop a national electronic KYC (e-KYC) system, officially described as 'the country's first step to achieving electronic KYC processes'; current processes were described by the Central Bank Deputy Governor as 'manual, paper-based'. The national ID card is accepted by banks as a supporting document for manual identity checks (Smile ID), but the digital ID system itself does not yet enable electronic KYC packet collection. The original score of 2 (Yes) conflated document acceptance with system-level enablement; revised down to 1 (No) on the basis of the fetched DPI Map entry and three independent 2025 news reports of the same Central Bank initiative.
revised_comments: The national identity card is accepted by commercial banks as a supporting identity document for manual Know Your Customer (KYC) checks, in line with Section 19 of the Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism (Prevention) (Amendment) Act, 2016. However, the digital ID system itself does not yet enable electronic KYC packet collection: KYC processes remain manual and paper-based. The Central Bank of Eswatini launched a national electronic KYC (e-KYC) initiative in late 2025, convening banks, regulators and government ministries to develop a centralised digital verification registry, described as the country's first step toward electronic KYC, but this had not been operationalised as of the most recent reporting.

Definition: Whether the ID authority and system are subject to general oversight of the courts and judicial review
Value Name: Yes, but not specific to ID
Comments: Eswatini's Data Protection Act 2022 allows data subjects to pursue civil actions for damages in court and lodge complaints with the Communications Commission. There are general judicial mechanisms for redress but no ID-specific judicial oversight mechanism. DPI Map records 'Legally binding redress mechanism: NA' under national identity. General rule-of-law courts can hear data protection complaints under the 2022 Act.
revision_notes: Confirmed via primary Act text: the Data Protection Act, 2022 provides for civil remedies through the courts (s.43) and Commission-led complaint investigation (s.34); no ID-specific judicial review mechanism was identified. DPI Map corroborates 'Legally binding redress mechanism: NA' for national identity. Score of 2 (Yes, but not specific to ID) confirmed.
revised_comments: General judicial oversight applies to identity-related data disputes through the ordinary courts and through complaints to the Eswatini Communications Commission acting as Data Protection Authority under the Data Protection Act, 2022, which provides for civil remedies and Commission-led investigation of complaints. There is no identity-specific judicial review mechanism; oversight relies on general data protection and administrative law channels.

Definition: Whether the civil registration and digital ID systems are integrated
Comments: The UNDP 2024 DRA notes 'mixed expert assessment of digital transformation of the civil registration, indicating inconsistent implementation of digitisation initiatives.' ICAP (2022) confirms CRVS activities are strengthened with the 5-year CRVS Strategic Plan 2022-2027. ECA notes digitisation of identity management 'is providing an opportunity for linkage with birth and death registration' but this is still in progress. The World Bank Digital Economy Diagnostic notes an integrated CRVS-NPR system exists but linkages are partial.
revision_notes: Confirmed: the CRVS Strategic Plan 2022-2027 and an ongoing CRVS improvement mentorship programme with the UN Economic Commission for Africa show active efforts to strengthen and digitise civil registration, with the Ministry of Home Affairs as central database agency for both CRVS and identity management (the 'closing of the tap' initiative links birth registration to the population register). UNDP DRA (2024) still finds 'mixed expert assessment' of CRVS digital transformation, indicating integration remains partial rather than full. Score of 2 (Partial integration) confirmed.
revised_comments: Eswatini's civil registration and digital identity systems are partially integrated. The Ministry of Home Affairs operates as the central database agency for both civil registration and the National Population Register, and the 'closing of the tap' initiative links birth registration directly to population register entries. The five-year Civil Registration and Vital Statistics Strategic Plan (2022-2027) and an ongoing CRVS improvement mentorship programme with the UN Economic Commission for Africa are strengthening this integration, but independent assessment in 2024 still finds inconsistent implementation of civil registration digitisation.

Definition: Whether procedural rules for collection, storage, and sharing of ID-related personal data are publicly available and established
Comments: The Data Protection Act 2022 establishes partial rules for data sharing: it requires explicit consent for data transfers, mandates secure measures for trans-border data flows (full within SADC, conditional outside). However, DPI Map records 'Terms of data storage and sharing available: NO' and 'Data handling terms exist: NO' specifically for the ID system, indicating ID-specific sharing rules are not yet publicly available. General data sharing rules exist under the DPA 2022 but are not ID-specific.
revision_notes: Confirmed via primary Act text (ss.9-16, 32-33) and DPI Map (Oct 2024), which records 'Terms of data storage and sharing available: NO' and 'Data handling terms exist: NO' specifically for the identity system. General consent and cross-border transfer rules exist under the Data Protection Act, 2022, but no ID-specific data-sharing framework is publicly documented. Score of 2 (Partially available) confirmed.
revised_comments: General rules for the collection, processing and cross-border transfer of personal data are set out in the Data Protection Act, 2022, which requires consent for data transfers and secure handling of trans-border flows. However, no identity-system-specific data-sharing agreement or procedural framework is publicly published; ID-related data sharing is governed only by these general provisions rather than by dedicated identity-system rules.

Definition: Whether national data protection legislation exists and covers personal data linked to the ID system
Comments: The Data Protection Act No. 5 of 2022 came into force on 4 March 2022. It governs the collection, processing, storage, and disclosure of personal data, aligned with SADC standards. It applies to both public and private entities and covers biometric data. DPI Map records 'National Data Protection Act exists: YES'.
revision_notes: Confirmed via the official Government Gazette text of the Data Protection Act, 2022 (Act No. 5 of 2022, in force 4 March 2022). The Act defines 'biometric' data (s.2) as including fingerprinting, DNA analysis, retinal scanning and voice recognition, and regulates it as sensitive personal information, directly covering ID-linked biometric data. Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed.
revised_comments: The Data Protection Act, 2022 (Act No. 5 of 2022) came into force on 4 March 2022 and governs the collection, processing, storage and disclosure of personal data by public and private entities. The Act explicitly defines and regulates biometric data (fingerprinting, DNA analysis, retinal scanning, voice recognition) as sensitive personal information, providing legal coverage for data linked to the national identity system.

Definition: Whether a Data Protection Authority or similar body regulates ID data collection and sharing by the ID system
Comments: The Eswatini Communications Commission (ESCCOM) is designated as the Data Protection Authority (EDPA) under the Data Protection Act 2022. It is empowered to monitor compliance, investigate violations, issue codes of conduct, and impose fines up to E5 million. DPI Map records 'Data leak disclosure process exists: YES'. The World Bank notes the Data Protection Office still needs full operationalisation.
revision_notes: Confirmed via primary Act text: ESCCOM is designated the data protection regulator (ss.5-8) with powers to investigate, sanction and enforce compliance (ss.34-53). World Bank's July 2025 Eswatini Economic Update notes the dedicated Data Protection Office still requires full operationalisation, indicating the oversight mandate exists in law but institutional capacity continues to develop. Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed.
revised_comments: The Eswatini Communications Commission (ESCCOM) is designated as the data protection regulator under the Data Protection Act, 2022, with statutory powers to investigate complaints, issue codes of conduct and impose sanctions of up to E5 million. The World Bank's 2025 Eswatini Economic Update notes that the Data Protection Office still requires full operationalisation, indicating that while the oversight mandate exists in law, institutional capacity continues to be built.

Definition: Whether the digital ID credential serves as legal proof of an individual's identity as codified in law
Comments: The National Identity Card (issued since 2003 by the Ministry of Home Affairs) is the primary legal proof of identity in Eswatini. It is compulsory for all citizens (Wikipedia). It is used for banking KYC, SIM registration, gambling ID checks, and other legal purposes. The card includes name, date of birth, chief code, and Personal Identity Number (PIN) and serves as legal proof of identity.
revision_notes: Fetched the primary legislation: the Identification Order, 1998 (EswatiniLII), which establishes the National Population Register and requires the Registrar to issue identity documents to all persons who have attained age 16, making it the codified legal basis for identity proof - a more precise primary source than the Wikipedia reference used originally (which stated cards issued 'since 2003'). Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed; year corrected to 1998, the year of the founding legislation.
revised_comments: The national identity document, established under the Identification Order, 1998, is the codified legal proof of identity in Eswatini. The Order requires the Registrar to compile and maintain a National Population Register and to issue identity documents to all persons who have attained the age of 16, making possession compulsory. The identity number and document are used as the basis for banking KYC, SIM card registration and other legally mandated identity checks.

Definition: Whether formal legislation (act, law, regulation) governs digital identity including identification acts, digital ID laws, or equivalent legislation
Comments: Eswatini enacted four pieces of ICT legislation in 2022 with certificates of urgency: the Electronic Communications Act, Electronic Communications Transactions Act, Computer Crime and Cybercrime Act, and Data Protection Act. The national ID is governed under civil registration law (Ministry of Home Affairs). ECDPM 2023 confirms Eswatini has regulations on civil registration emphasising identity Acts. DPI Map records 'ID or Civil Registry Act: YES'.
revision_notes: The core legal framework governing national/digital identity is the Identification Order, 1998, which establishes the Population Register and identity document issuance, enrolment and fee-setting powers - a more precise primary source than the 2022 ICT Acts cited originally, which regulate data protection and electronic transactions more broadly rather than identity specifically. Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed; primary identity legislation and year corrected to 1998.
revised_comments: Digital identity in Eswatini is governed by the Identification Order, 1998, which establishes the National Population Register, the Registrar's functions, enrolment and issuance procedures, and fee-setting powers for identity documents. This foundational identification law is complemented by more recent ICT-sector legislation enacted in 2022, including the Data Protection Act, Electronic Communications Act, Electronic Communications Transactions Act, and Computer Crime and Cybercrime Act, which together provide the wider legal environment for digital identity and data governance.

Definition: Whether identity records are stored in electronic/digital format versus paper-based records
Comments: The World Bank 2021 Digital Economy Diagnostic notes Eswatini has an integrated civil registration and national identification system based on the National Population Register (NPR). The Ministry of Home Affairs centrally stores ID data electronically. The UNDP 2024 DRA notes digitisation of the identity management component is ongoing and provides opportunity for linkage with birth and death registration. The National Data Centre is housed at the Royal Science and Technology Park.
revision_notes: World Bank Digital Economy Diagnostic (2022) confirms an integrated, centrally-stored National Population Register held electronically by the Ministry of Home Affairs. Recent reporting (Africa Business Insight, May 2026) on a months-long ID card production outage caused by a 'computer system failure' further evidences the underlying system is computerised (production has since resumed). Score of 3 (Digital) confirmed.
revised_comments: Identity records are held in an electronic National Population Register maintained centrally by the Ministry of Home Affairs, with data storage housed at the National Data Centre at the Royal Science and Technology Park. The system is computerised rather than paper-based, as illustrated by a 2025-2026 nationwide service disruption caused by a computer system failure that halted ID card production for several months before being resolved in mid-2026.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for opening bank accounts and accessing financial services
Comments: The national ID card is accepted (not formally mandatory) for banking and financial services KYC. Smile ID confirms it is the primary KYC document and banks access the civil registry for identity verification. The APC report notes banks see 'huge benefits' from e-KYC using national ID. The 2016 AML/KYC law requires identity verification but allows passports and other documents too, making the national ID accepted but not exclusively mandatory.
revision_notes: Confirmed via Smile ID (national ID card as primary KYC document), APC (banks access civil registry for verification), and a commercial bank's own published KYC document list (SwaziBank), which accepts 'Identity card/Passport (mandatory)' alongside other supporting documents rather than exclusively requiring the national ID. Score of 2 (Accepted but not mandatory) confirmed.
revised_comments: The national identity card is widely accepted by commercial banks as the primary Know Your Customer (KYC) document, alongside passports and other identification, under Section 19 of the Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism (Prevention) (Amendment) Act, 2016. It is not the sole legally mandated document for account opening, since passports are also accepted.

Definition: Whether credentials are issued free of charge
Comments: The 2021 Ministry of Home Affairs fee schedule shows the first ID enrolment within the first 3 months of turning 16 is free. However, for those enrolling at age 17-25 a fee of E100 applies, and E250 for ages 26 and above. Replacement of a lost/destroyed ID costs E300. The credential is effectively free for timely first enrolment at age 16 but has costs for late or replacement issuance. Value=1 (No cost for initial enrollment when done on time).
revision_notes: Fetched the Ministry of Home Affairs' official fee schedule (effective 1 March 2021), which confirms 'First ID Enrolment within first three (3) months after turning sixteen (16) years' is Free (reduced from E25). Fees apply only to late first enrolment (E100 for ages 17-25, E250 for 26+), replacement of lost/destroyed cards (E300), and corrections (E300). Since the standard/primary issuance pathway is free, the original score of 1 (No) contradicted the evidence cited in its own comment and is corrected to 2 (Yes).
revised_comments: Identity cards are issued free of charge for citizens who enrol within three months of turning 16, under the Ministry of Home Affairs fee schedule effective 1 March 2021. Fees apply only to late first enrolment (E100 for ages 17-25, E250 for those 26 and above) and to replacement of lost or destroyed cards (E300), which function as penalties for delay or loss rather than standard issuance charges.

Definition: Age in years at which an individual becomes eligible to register for digital ID
Comments: The Eswatini government fee schedule (Ministry of Home Affairs, 2021) shows first ID enrolment is for those turning 16 years old (free within first 3 months of turning 16, then fees apply up to age 25). Wikipedia lists Eswatini's national ID as 'compulsory for all citizens'. The minimum enrolment age of 16 maps to Value=1 (>17 bracket is closest; 16 falls in >17 category as the cut-off is above 17).
revision_notes: The Identification Order, 1998 (ss.7-9) and the Ministry of Home Affairs fee schedule both confirm the enrolment age is 16 years. Per the variable's scale (1=>17; 2=10-17; 3=6-10; 4=1-5; 5=<1), an eligibility age of 16 falls within the 10-17 bracket (Value=2), not the >17 bracket (Value=1) used originally - the original entry's own comment cites age 16 but misapplies the scale. Corrected to 2.
revised_comments: Individuals become eligible to enrol for a national identity document at age 16, as set out in the Identification Order, 1998, and confirmed by the Ministry of Home Affairs fee schedule, which specifies free enrolment within three months of turning 16.

Definition: Whether registration for digital ID is mandatory, optional, or mandatory for specific groups
Comments: Wikipedia records Eswatini's national ID as 'compulsory for all citizens of the Kingdom of Eswatini'. The Ministry of Home Affairs fee schedule confirms enrolment and card collection obligations. Enrollment is mandatory for all eligible citizens.
revision_notes: The Identification Order, 1998 confirms compulsory enrolment for every person who has attained the age of 16 (ss.7-9), corroborated by Wikipedia's classification of Eswatini as having compulsory ID cards. Score of 3 (Mandatory for all) confirmed; primary legal source and year corrected to 1998.
revised_comments: Enrolment for a national identity document is mandatory for all persons who have attained the age of 16, under the Identification Order, 1998. The Ministry of Home Affairs' fee structure, which waives fees for timely enrolment at 16 but charges increasing fees for later enrolment, is designed to encourage compliance with this mandatory requirement.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for accessing public healthcare services
Comments: Eswatini uses the national ID number as the Unique Patient Identifier (UPI) in its health information system according to a 2016 health informatics study (PMC). However, this is accepted but not universally mandatory for all healthcare access (patients without ID can still be seen). The 2024 DRA identifies health services as an area for further digital expansion.
revision_notes: The originally cited PMC source could not be accessed (blocked by an automated bot-check), but its 2016 claim that identity/population-register numbers function as a unique patient identifier is corroborated by more recent evidence: Jembi Health Systems (January 2026) confirms integration of Eswatini's Population Registry into a Master Patient Index to strengthen patient identification across health facilities, and Data.FI reporting (April 2026) confirms the Client Management Information System (CMIS), live in 73% of public health facilities, uses a unique ID number for patient records. Use is for identification/deduplication rather than as a gatekeeping requirement for care access. Score of 2 (Accepted but not mandatory) confirmed.
revised_comments: Eswatini's health information system draws on the national Population Registry and associated identity numbers to strengthen unique patient identification. The Client Management Information System (CMIS), an electronic medical record now live in 73% of public health facilities, uses a unique ID number for patient records and to prevent duplicate registrations. Identity documentation supports patient identification and record linkage but is not a mandatory precondition for receiving care.

Definition: Whether non-nationals including refugees, asylum seekers, and permanent residents are eligible to register
Comments: The Ministry of Home Affairs 2021 fee schedule includes an 'ID extension non-Swazi' category (E150 fee), indicating that non-nationals can obtain some form of ID extension or permit. SIM registration regulations (Legal Notice No. 26 of 2016) required registration for 'both local citizens and non-Swazi individuals'. This indicates some non-nationals are eligible for certain ID documents, but full national ID eligibility for all non-nationals is not established.
revision_notes: Confirmed via the Ministry of Home Affairs' identity card service page, which sets out distinct application pathways for refugees, asylum seekers ('non-Swazi ID') and other non-nationals holding valid temporary residence, work or student permits, and via an Alliance for Financial Inclusion (2022) report confirming refugees/asylum seekers aged 16+ can obtain refugee or non-Swazi IDs. Coverage is category-specific and conditional on immigration/protection status rather than universal, so 'Some' remains the appropriate score. Score of 2 (Some) confirmed.
revised_comments: Several categories of non-nationals are eligible to register for identity documentation in Eswatini, including refugees and asylum seekers aged 16 and above, who receive a 'non-Swazi ID' or refugee ID via the Refugees Department, and other non-citizens holding valid temporary residence, work or student permits. Eligibility is conditional on immigration or protection status rather than universal for all non-nationals.

Definition: Percentage of eligible population that has been issued or registered with digital ID credentials
Comments: The UNDP 2024 Digital Readiness Assessment reports that 88% of adults (over age 15) held a government-issued ID during 2021-2022, which is above the sub-Saharan Africa average of 78%. 88% falls in the 70-89% band (Value=4). The national ID is compulsory for all citizens, and the government has decentralised registration to all tinkhundla (local government units) to improve coverage.
revision_notes: UNDP Digital Readiness Assessment (published November 2024, using 2021-2022 survey data) confirms 88% of adults aged 15+ hold a government-issued ID, above the sub-Saharan Africa average of 78%, falling in the 70-89% band (Value=4). A more recent World Bank DPI diagnostic (2025) notes a gender gap in ID possession linked to slightly lower female birth registration rates but does not supersede the 88% national estimate. No more recent national coverage figure was identified. Score of 4 (70-89%) confirmed.
revised_comments: An estimated 88% of Eswatini's adult population (aged 15 and above) held a government-issued identity document during 2021-2022, according to the UNDP/Ministry of ICT Digital Readiness Assessment, above the 78% average recorded across sub-Saharan Africa. The World Bank has noted a modest gender gap in ID possession, linked to slightly lower birth registration rates among girls than boys.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for SIM card activation and mobile service registration
Comments: SIM card registration is mandatory in Eswatini under Legal Notice No. 26 of 2016 issued by the Minister of ICT under the Swaziland Communications Commission Act. MTN Eswatini confirms customers must bring their 'National ID/Passport and Proof of Residence' and failure to register results in disconnection. The Prepaid SIM Wiki confirms Eswatini/Swaziland requires registration at point-of-sale.
revision_notes: Confirmed via MTN Eswatini's own FAQ page (requires National ID/Passport and Proof of Residence; failure to register results in disconnection) and the APC report's confirmation of Legal Notice No. 26 of 2016 issued under the Swaziland Communications Commission Act, 2013. Score of 3 (Mandatory) confirmed.
revised_comments: SIM card registration is mandatory in Eswatini under Legal Notice No. 26 of 2016, issued under the Swaziland Communications Commission Act, 2013. Mobile operators require customers to present a National ID or passport plus proof of residence at the point of sale, and unregistered SIM cards are subject to disconnection.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for registering for social assistance programs and accessing social services
Comments: The national ID is used to access social services such as the Old Age Grant (age 60+) and other social assistance programs administered by the Deputy Prime Minister's Office. The 2025 social security analysis notes challenges with 'incomplete civil registration systems and identification' for social protection, suggesting the national ID is accepted but not always enforced as mandatory for all social services. The government is developing a National Social Registry.
revision_notes: Fetched the Ministry-run Social Welfare Department page, the primary source for grant application requirements. It lists 'National Identity card' (unconditionally) alongside 'Proof of income or dividends (if any)' (conditionally) as the required documents to apply for the Elderly Grant, and states 'NB - No cash without ID card' for payment collection. This is a direct, authoritative requirement for one of Eswatini's core social assistance programmes, not merely an accepted-but-optional document. Original score of 2 is not supported by this primary evidence; revised up to 3 (Mandatory).
revised_comments: The national identity card is a mandatory requirement for accessing Eswatini's social assistance programmes. The Ministry of Home Affairs-administered Social Welfare Department requires applicants for the Elderly Grant to present a National Identity Card when applying at a Tinkhundla centre, and explicitly states that cash payments cannot be collected without an ID card. Identity documentation is similarly used to track beneficiaries of other social grants, including the Orphans and Vulnerable Children education grant, via a Personal Identity Number.
